lines.text: Lesson nine: fees, spread and slippage.
The small costs that can turn a win into a loss.
Here's a tiny trade: 0.01 BTC. The price on the chart goes from 60,000 to 60,080.
On the chart, that looks like a gain of 0.80 USDT. Easy money?
Not so fast. Three costs are waiting: fees, spread and slippage.
A trading fee is charged each time an order fills, as a percentage of the position value.
Like a booking fee on a ticket: you pay it every time, whether things go well or not.
0.01 BTC at 60,000 is 600 USDT. At 0.05%, the fee is 0.30 USDT, on entry and again on exit.
Many exchanges charge two rates. A taker order fills at once against the book, like a market order.
A maker order waits in the book, like a limit order, and adds to it. Makers often pay less.
In this example: maker 0.02%, taker 0.05%. Real rates vary by exchange and account.
The spread is the gap between the best ask and the best bid.
Like a money changer: one price to buy from them, a lower price to sell back.
Ask 60,005, bid 59,995: spread 10. Buy and sell at once, and you lose 0.10 USDT on 0.01 BTC.
Slippage, from T07: the fill is worse than the price you expected.
Say each market order slips 10 USDT per BTC, on the way in and on the way out.
That is 20 per BTC, or 0.20 USDT on 0.01 BTC.
Futures have one more cost: funding. It's a regular payment between long and short traders.
It's separate from trading fees. You may pay it, or receive it, depending on the rate.
Example: a 0.01% rate on 600 USDT is 0.06 USDT, each funding time. T13 covers it.
Now let's add it all up for our tiny trade.
Chart gain: plus 0.80. Spread: minus 0.10. Slippage: minus 0.20.
Fees on entry and exit: minus 0.60 USDT.
Net result: minus 0.10 USDT. A gross winner became a net loser.
Funding is left out here, because this trade was closed within minutes.
The break-even move is how far price must move just to cover your costs.
Fees alone: 2 × 0.05% = 0.10%. On 60,000, that's 60 USDT per BTC.
Add spread and slippage, and it's about 90 USDT per BTC, or 0.15%, before you make anything.
A common mistake: fees look tiny, so people ignore them.
But 20 small trades at 0.60 USDT of fees each cost 12 USDT, win or lose.
Small, frequent trades feel the costs most. Count them before you trade.
Your turn. Buy 0.01 BTC at 60,000, sell at 60,040. Fees: 0.30 USDT on each side.
Ignore spread and slippage. What is the gross result, and the net? Pause if you need to.
Gross: 40 × 0.01 = plus 0.40 USDT. Fees: 0.60. Net: minus 0.20 USDT.
A winner on the chart, a loser in your account.
Before any trade, check your real costs.
Your actual fee rate and account tier. The spread right now. How deep the book is.
The funding rate and time. And does the move you expect beat the break-even move?
If not, NO_TRADE is the sensible choice.
This lesson used a simple model, with example numbers.
Real fees depend on your exchange and account tier. Check them before you act.
Fees are charged on the full position value, not just the money you put in.
And slippage grows in fast markets.
Let's recap.
Fees are charged on entry and exit, as a percentage of position value.
Spread and slippage quietly worsen your prices. Funding is a separate futures cost.
Check yourself: the move you expect is smaller than the break-even move. What do you do?
Don't trade. Choose WAIT, or NO_TRADE.
Well done! That completes Phase 2. Next up, T10: a tour of an exchange platform.
